questions.question: Which statement about the meaning of USP <71> sterility test results is correct?

options.A: A passing result proves the entire batch has been sterilized, with no further need to rely on process validation or environmental monitoring
options.B: A passing result only means that no contaminating microorganisms were found in the samples examined under the test conditions
options.C: The test is mainly intended to replace validation of the sterilization or aseptic process, so validation reports can be omitted
options.D: A passing result means no microorganisms are present anywhere in the batch, including containers that were not sampled

questions.explanation: The chapter states explicitly that these pharmacopeial procedures are not by themselves designed to ensure that a batch is sterile; sterility is achieved mainly through validation of the sterilization process or the aseptic processing procedures. A pass only means that no contaminating microorganisms were found in the samples examined under the test conditions.

questions.question: Which statement about Fluid Thioglycollate Medium (FTM) and Soybean–Casein Digest Medium (SCDM) is correct?

options.A: FTM is mainly for fungi and aerobic bacteria, incubated at 22.5 ± 2.5°
options.B: SCDM is mainly for anaerobic bacteria, incubated at 30–35°
options.C: FTM is mainly for anaerobic bacteria (it can also detect aerobic bacteria), incubated at 30–35°
options.D: FTM and SCDM are both incubated at 30–35°, differing only in the pH of the formulation

questions.explanation: FTM is intended primarily for anaerobic bacteria but can also detect aerobic bacteria, and is incubated at 30–35°; SCDM is suitable for fungi and aerobic bacteria and is incubated at 22.5 ± 2.5°. The statements "FTM for fungi and aerobic bacteria at 22.5 ± 2.5°" and "SCDM for anaerobic bacteria at 30–35°" swap the uses and temperatures of the two media.
questions.reference: USP <71> Culture Media and Incubation Temperatures

questions.question: Which requirement for the Growth Promotion Test of culture media is correct?

options.A: Test every batch of medium, inoculate not more than 100 cfu, and use cultures not more than 5 passages from the original master seed-lot
options.B: Test only once at annual qualification, inoculate not more than 1000 cfu, with no limit on the number of culture passages
options.C: Test every batch of medium, inoculate not less than 100 cfu, and use cultures not more than 10 passages from the original master seed-lot
options.D: Test only media prepared in-house, inoculate not more than 100 cfu, with no limit on the number of culture passages

questions.explanation: GPT is performed on each lot of ready-prepared medium and each batch of medium prepared from dehydrated medium or ingredients, using a small inoculum (not more than 100 cfu) and a seed-lot system so that cultures are not more than five passages from the original master seed-lot; the medium must show clearly visible growth of the organisms.
questions.reference: USP <71> Growth Promotion Test of Aerobes, Anaerobes, and Fungi

questions.question: A penicillin-type injection is to be sterility tested by Direct Inoculation. How should the media be adjusted, and how is a sufficient amount of β-lactamase confirmed?

options.A: Use a higher concentration of antibiotic neutralizer and confirm neutralization with Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the challenge organism
options.B: Dilute the sample with Fluid K and confirm recovery with Aspergillus brasiliensis as the challenge organism
options.C: Shorten the medium incubation time to 5 days and confirm growth with Bacillus subtilis as the challenge organism
options.D: Aseptically add a sufficient amount of β-lactamase and confirm growth with fewer than 100 cfu of S. aureus

questions.explanation: For direct inoculation, a sufficient amount of β-lactamase is aseptically added to the FTM and SCDM; alternatively, in an area completely separate from sterility testing, challenge with fewer than 100 cfu of S. aureus, and typical growth demonstrates that the β-lactamase concentration is adequate.
questions.reference: USP <71> Culture Media and Incubation Temperatures › Media for Penicillins or Cephalosporins

questions.question: An injection contains lecithin and is to be sterility tested by membrane filtration. Which diluting and rinsing fluid should be chosen, and how does it differ from Fluid A?

options.A: Fluid A, because it is specifically intended for oily or lecithin-containing products
options.B: Fluid D, made by adding 1 mL of polysorbate 80 per L of Fluid A
options.C: Fluid D, made by adding 10 g of polysorbate 80 per L of Fluid A
options.D: Fluid K, made by adding β-lactamase to Fluid A

questions.explanation: Fluid D is used for products containing lecithin or oil and for devices labeled as having a sterile pathway; it consists of Fluid A plus 1 mL of polysorbate 80 per L. Fluid K contains 10 g/L of polysorbate 80 but has its own separate formulation and is not made by adding β-lactamase.
questions.reference: USP <71> Diluting and Rinsing Fluids for Membrane Filtration › Fluid D

questions.question: A batch of liquid injection is filled at 20 mL per vial. Per Table 2, what is the minimum quantity per vial to use for each medium (unless otherwise justified)?
questions.explanation: For liquids in containers of 1–40 mL, the minimum quantity is half the contents of the container, but not less than 1 mL, so a 20-mL vial requires at least 10 mL. The 20 mL figure is the quantity Table 2 specifies for containers greater than 40 mL and not more than 100 mL.
questions.reference: USP <71> Test for Sterility of the Product to be Examined › Number of Articles to Be Tested, Table 2 (Liquids, 1–40 mL)

questions.question: A batch of ordinary parenteral preparation (not a large-volume infusion) comprises 300 containers. Per Table 3, what is the minimum number of containers to test for each medium?
questions.explanation: For parenteral preparations with a batch size of more than 100 but not more than 500 containers, a minimum of 10 containers is tested per medium. The figure of 4 is the lower bound of "10% or 4 containers, whichever is greater" for batches not exceeding 100; the figure of 20 is the upper cap of "2% or 20 containers, whichever is less" for batches above 500.
questions.reference: USP <71> Test for Sterility of the Product to be Examined › Number of Articles to Be Tested, Table 3 (Parenteral preparations)

questions.question: For a product with antimicrobial properties tested by membrane filtration, the Method Suitability Test shows that rinsing with 5 × 100 mL still does not completely eliminate the antimicrobial activity. How should rinsing be handled in the actual test?

options.A: Increase the number of rinses until the antimicrobial activity is completely eliminated
options.B: Double the volume of each rinse, still rinsing 5 times
options.C: Rinse only once, but increase the polysorbate 80 concentration of the rinse fluid
options.D: Still do not exceed a washing cycle of 5 × 100 mL per filter

questions.explanation: The chapter requires products with antimicrobial activity to be rinsed at least 3 times, each with the volume used in the Method Suitability Test, and even if validation shows that the cycle cannot completely eliminate the antimicrobial activity, the washing cycle must not exceed 5 × 100 mL per filter.
questions.reference: USP <71> Test for Sterility of the Product to be Examined › Membrane Filtration › Aqueous Solutions

questions.question: In direct inoculation, how does the handling of oily liquids differ from that of ointments and creams?

options.A: Both are added directly to medium containing an emulsifier, with no dilution and no transfer to another medium
options.B: Oily liquids use medium with added emulsifier; ointments and creams are emulsified and diluted about 1 in 10 and then transferred to medium without emulsifier
options.C: Oily liquids are diluted to 1% before use; ointments and creams use medium with added emulsifier, without dilution
options.D: Both are first rinsed with Fluid K and then transferred to medium without emulsifier, with no emulsification

questions.explanation: Oily liquids use medium to which a suitable emulsifier (for example, 10 g/L polysorbate 80) has been added; ointments and creams are first diluted about 1 in 10 with an emulsifier in a sterile diluent and then transferred to medium without emulsifier. The 1% dilution is the approach for ointments with a greasy base using isopropyl myristate in membrane filtration.
questions.reference: USP <71> Test for Sterility of the Product to be Examined › Direct Inoculation of the Culture Medium › Oily Liquids; Ointments and Creams

questions.question: Which statement about the membrane filters used in membrane filtration is correct?

options.A: Nominal pore size not greater than 0.45 µm; cellulose nitrate for aqueous, oily, and weakly alcoholic solutions, and cellulose acetate for strongly alcoholic solutions
options.B: Nominal pore size not greater than 0.22 µm; cellulose acetate for aqueous and oily solutions, cellulose nitrate for strongly alcoholic solutions, and pre-wetted with a 0.22 µm filter beforehand
options.C: Nominal pore size not greater than 0.45 µm; cellulose nitrate always used for aqueous, oily, and alcoholic solutions
options.D: Any pore size, as long as the filter is about 50 mm in diameter, sterilized, and shown to be compatible with the product

questions.explanation: The nominal pore size of the filter must not be greater than 0.45 µm, and its effectiveness in retaining microorganisms must have been established; cellulose nitrate is used, for example, for aqueous, oily, and weakly alcoholic solutions, and cellulose acetate, for example, for strongly alcoholic solutions. Specially adapted filters may be needed for certain products such as antibiotics.
questions.reference: USP <71> Test for Sterility of the Product to be Examined › Membrane Filtration (filter selection paragraph)

questions.question: When the test product renders the medium turbid so that the presence or absence of microbial growth cannot be readily determined by visual examination, how should it be handled?

options.A: Judge it as non-compliant directly, because turbidity indicates microbial growth, with no need for subculture
options.B: Centrifuge the medium on day 7 and re-read it visually to remove the turbidity caused by the product
options.C: Extend the original incubation to 28 days and read, with no subculture; if still turbid at 28 days it fails, with a weekly visual check recorded
options.D: After 14 days of incubation, transfer not less than 1 mL of each to fresh medium of the same type, and incubate the original and transfer vessels for not less than 4 days

questions.explanation: When turbid, not less than 1 mL of each medium is transferred to fresh medium of the same type 14 days after the start of incubation, and the original and transfer vessels are incubated for not less than 4 days before being read for growth. Turbidity alone cannot be taken directly as a failure.
questions.reference: USP <71> Observation and Interpretation of Results (turbid media)

questions.question: In a sterility test batch, growth appeared in the medium and was identified as a common skin organism. Environmental monitoring, review of operating procedures, and negative controls revealed no deficiencies, and QC believes it was "probably operator contamination." Can the test be declared invalid?

options.A: Yes, skin organisms always originate from the operator, so the identification alone is enough to declare the test invalid
options.B: Yes, provided the QA manager agrees in writing and the test is repeated, with no other evidence needed
options.C: No, one of the four invalidity conditions must be met, and the fourth requires that growth be clearly attributable to a material or technique deficiency
options.D: No, because a sterility test can never be declared invalid and repeated, regardless of the investigation outcome

questions.explanation: A test may be considered invalid only if one of four conditions applies: a deficiency in monitoring, a deficiency in procedures, growth in the negative controls, or, after identification, growth of the organism that can be clearly attributed to a deficiency in materials or technique. Without evidence, a presumption is not enough, and the product fails the sterility test.
questions.reference: USP <71> Observation and Interpretation of Results (invalid test conditions 1–4)

questions.question: A sterility test has been validly declared invalid. How should the repeat test be performed and judged?

options.A: Use only half the number of units; the product fails only if the repeat also shows growth, and passes if there is no growth, taking the strictest result as final
options.B: Use the same number of units as in the original test; the product passes if there is no growth in the repeat and fails if there is growth
options.C: Use twice the number of units; the product passes as long as most units show no growth, and a minority with growth can be disregarded
options.D: Repeat the test until a result with no growth is obtained, taking the last result as final

questions.explanation: After the test is declared invalid, it is repeated with the same number of units as in the original test. If no microbial growth is found in the repeat test, the product complies with the sterility test; if growth is found, it fails, and there is no opportunity for a second repeat.
questions.reference: USP <71> Observation and Interpretation of Results (repeat test)

questions.question: For parenteral preparations tested by membrane filtration, what is the principle for sample quantity and dilution?

options.A: Use the whole contents of the container where possible, not less than the quantity in Table 2, diluting to about 100 mL if necessary
options.B: Always use only the minimum quantity in Table 2 and dilute to about 500 mL to reduce antimicrobial effects
options.C: Use only half the Table 2 quantity and do not dilute so as not to reduce detection, shortening the filtration time
options.D: Use the whole contents without dilution so as not to alter the product, with no lower limit on the volume filtered

questions.explanation: In membrane filtration, the whole contents of the container are used where possible, but not less than the quantity in Table 2, diluting if necessary to about 100 mL with a suitable sterile solution (such as Fluid A). Using the minimum quantity is not the principle, and the dilution target is also about 100 mL.
questions.reference: USP <71> Application of the Test to Parenteral Preparations, Ophthalmic, and Other Noninjectable Preparations (membrane filtration paragraph)

questions.topic: Same sample for bacteria and fungi
questions.question: The quantity in a single container is not enough to supply both the FTM and the SCDM tests. How should this be handled?

options.A: Test only FTM, because it can also detect aerobic bacteria and fungi, so the SCDM test can be omitted and no medium needs to be reserved
options.B: Take one container from each of two different batches, inoculate each into one medium, and read them separately
options.C: Extrapolate the result from the smaller quantity and treat both media as tested, with no further sampling
options.D: The bacterial and fungal tests must still use the same sample, using the contents of two or more containers to inoculate the different media

questions.explanation: The sterility tests for bacteria and fungi are performed on the same sample of the product; when the quantity in a single container or the number of containers is insufficient, the contents of two or more containers may be used to inoculate the different media. The other options either omit one medium or use samples from different batches, neither of which is permitted.
questions.reference: USP <71> Application of the Test to Parenteral Preparations, Ophthalmic, and Other Noninjectable Preparations (same sample paragraph)
